questions.title: Cracking
questions.text: Define the term **computer system cracking**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Gaining unauthorised access to a computer system / network / data (1)
- usually with malicious intent, e.g. to steal, change or damage data (1)
scheme.model_answer: Breaking into a computer system or its data without permission, usually to steal, change or damage information.

questions.title: Types of hacker
questions.text: Match each type of hacker to its description.

right.text: Breaks in illegally for personal gain or to cause harm
Tests a system with the owner's permission to find weaknesses
Breaks in without permission but without criminal intent

scheme.mark_scheme: Black–R1, White–R2, Grey–R3. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Cracking methods
questions.text: Match each cracking method to its description.

right.text: Tries every possible password until one works
A fake e-mail tricks the user into entering a password on a false website
Database commands are typed into a web form
Secretly records the keys the user presses

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R1, L2–R2, L3–R3, L4–R4. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Ethical problems of cracking
questions.text: State **two** ethical problems that arise when a criminal cracks an online shop's database.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): customers' privacy is violated; identity theft; theft of money / card details; innocent customers harmed; loss of trust; confidential business data stolen; blackmail
scheme.model_answer: 1 Customers' private details are exposed, violating their privacy. 2 Stolen card details may be used to take customers' money.

questions.title: Analyse a hospital attack
questions.text: Analyse the problems that arise when a hospital's computer system is cracked and patients' records are stolen.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any three developed points (1 each): patients' confidential medical data exposed — privacy violated / discrimination / blackmail; records may be changed — wrong treatment endangers lives; systems unavailable — treatment delayed; hospital fined / loses reputation / patients lose trust; cost of recovery and security improvements
scheme.model_answer: Patients' medical histories could be published or sold, violating their privacy and possibly leading to blackmail or discrimination. If the attacker changes records, patients could receive the wrong medicine, which could endanger lives. The hospital may also be fined for failing to protect personal data and patients may stop trusting it.

questions.title: Only looking
questions.text: Accessing someone else's account without permission is legal as long as you do not change any data.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: Unauthorised access is itself an offence, whether or not data is changed.

questions.title: Protect against cracking
questions.text: The school database is always at risk of system cracking. Write **two** ways to protect against cracking.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Any two (1 each): enacting two-factor authentication; increasing password complexity; using SSL protocol; encrypting; hashing; limiting login attempts; firewall; access rights; updates
[max 2]
scheme.model_answer: 1 Use two-factor authentication. 2 Limit the number of login attempts.

questions.title: Stopping brute force
questions.text: Explain how **limiting the number of login attempts** protects an account against a brute-force attack.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A brute-force attack tries very many passwords one after another (1)
- after a few wrong attempts the account is locked / delayed, so the attacker cannot try enough passwords (1)
scheme.model_answer: A brute-force program tries thousands of passwords; if the account is locked after, say, five wrong attempts, the program cannot keep guessing until it finds the right one.

questions.title: Strongest password
questions.text: Which password is the most difficult to crack?

scheme.mark_scheme: C
scheme.explanation: It is long and mixes upper and lower case letters, digits and symbols, and is not a word or name.

questions.title: Authentication or authorisation
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row.

prefill: Entering a password and a code sent to a phone
A pupil can view but not change their marks
Scanning a fingerprint to log in
Only the accountant can open the salary folder

scheme.mark_scheme: 1 Authentication (1); 2 Authorisation (1); 3 Authentication (1); 4 Authorisation (1)

questions.title: Protect confidential data
questions.text: Give **two** measures that a company can take to protect confidential data from being stolen.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two from: encrypting data (1); granting limited access rights (1); blocking access from certain locations (1); keeping logs of user entries (1); 2FA; firewall; physical security
scheme.model_answer: 1 Encrypt the data. 2 Give each employee access only to the data they need.

questions.title: Hashing passwords
questions.text: Explain why a website should store **hashes** of passwords instead of the passwords themselves.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A hash is a one-way transformation — the password cannot be worked out from it (1)
- so if the database is stolen, the attacker does not get the users' actual passwords (1)

points.criterion: Stolen database does not reveal passwords

scheme.model_answer: Hashing is one-way, so the original password cannot be recovered from the hash; if crackers steal the database, they still do not have users' passwords.

questions.title: Types of malware
questions.text: Match each type of malware to its description.

right.text: Spreads by itself across a network without user action
Pretends to be useful software but opens a back door

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R1, L2–R2, L3–R3, L4–R4. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Virus vs worm
questions.text: Explain the difference between a **virus** and a **worm**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A virus attaches to a host file / program and spreads when that file is run or shared (needs user action) (1)
- A worm is a standalone program that copies itself across networks automatically (1)
scheme.model_answer: A virus needs a host file and spreads when a user runs or shares that file, whereas a worm is a separate program that spreads across networks on its own.

questions.title: Ransomware problems
questions.text: State **two** problems that ransomware can cause for a company.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): files cannot be opened / data loss; work stops — downtime / lost income; ransom payment / cost of recovery; customers' data leaked / fines; reputation damage; no guarantee files are returned after paying
scheme.model_answer: 1 Staff cannot open any files, so the company cannot work. 2 The company may lose money paying the ransom or restoring its systems.

questions.title: Trojans
questions.text: A Trojan horse usually gets onto a computer because the user installs it, believing it is useful software.

scheme.mark_scheme: True.

questions.title: Purpose of a privacy policy
questions.text: Explain the purpose of a **privacy policy** on a website.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- It tells users what personal data is collected and how it is used / stored / shared (1)
- so users can give informed consent / know their rights; it is required by law (1)
scheme.model_answer: It explains what personal data the website collects and how it is used, stored and shared, so users can decide whether to agree and know what rights they have.

questions.title: What a privacy policy contains
questions.text: Select **two** items that a privacy policy should contain.

options.content: Which personal data is collected and why
Whether data is shared with third parties
The programming language used for the website

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: Read a privacy policy
questions.text:
A fitness app's privacy policy says:

> *We collect your heart rate and location to measure your workouts. We may share anonymised data with research partners. Your data is stored for two years. You can download or delete your data at any time.*

Identify from the policy:

fields.label: Who the data is shared with

scheme.mark_scheme:
Data: heart rate and location (1)
Shared with: research partners (anonymised) (1)
Right: download / delete their data (1)
scheme.model_answer: Heart rate and location; anonymised data with research partners; the user can delete their data.

questions.title: Ransomware at a hospital
questions.text:
Ransomware encrypts all the computers in a city hospital. The attackers demand 50 000 dollars for the decryption key.

Analyse the problems caused by this attack and suggest how the hospital could have reduced its impact.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Problems (max 3): patient records unavailable — treatments / operations delayed, lives at risk; appointments cancelled / patients sent elsewhere; cost of ransom or recovery; data may also be stolen and leaked — privacy; reputation / trust; paying does not guarantee recovery and funds criminals
Prevention (max 2): regular offline / off-site backups; anti-virus and updates; staff training on phishing; network segmentation / firewall; limited access rights
[Max 4]
scheme.model_answer: Doctors cannot open patients' records, so operations are delayed and lives may be at risk. The hospital loses money either paying the ransom, which does not guarantee the files are returned, or restoring its systems, and patients may lose trust in it. If it had kept regular offline backups, it could have restored the files without paying, and updated anti-virus software and staff training against phishing e-mails would have made the infection less likely.

questions.title: Evaluate privacy policies
questions.text: A social network has 2 million users in Kazakhstan. Explain what its privacy policy should contain, and evaluate how well privacy policies actually protect users' personal data.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Contents (max 3): data collected; purpose; sharing with third parties / advertisers; storage period and location; security measures; user rights (access, correct, delete, withdraw consent); cookies; contact; changes
Evaluation (max 3): positive — legal requirement / accountability / informed consent / trust; negative — too long / legal language, users do not read them; must accept to use the service; policies change; does not guarantee actual security; data may still be hacked
A reasoned conclusion may gain credit within the maximum.
scheme.model_answer: The policy should state which personal data the network collects (profile, messages, location), why it collects it, whether it is shared with advertisers, how long it is kept and where it is stored, how it is protected, and the users' rights to see, correct and delete their data. Policies are useful because the law requires them and they make the company accountable, so users can give informed consent. However, most people never read them because they are long and full of legal terms, users must accept them to use the service, and the company can change them. A policy also does not prevent the data from being hacked, so it protects users only partly; strong security measures and enforcement by the law are also needed.

questions.title: Cracking a school database
questions.text: The school database stores pupils' personal data and marks. It is always at risk of system cracking.

parts.title: Ways to protect
parts.text: Write **two** ways to protect against cracking.

scheme.mark_scheme: Enacting two-factor authentication (1) Increasing password complexity (1) Use SSL protocol (1) Encrypting (1) Hashing (1) Limiting login attempts (1) [max 2]
scheme.model_answer: 1 Two-factor authentication. 2 Encrypting the data.

parts.title: Brute force
parts.text: Describe a **brute-force** attack and **one** way to prevent it.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A program tries every possible password / combination until the correct one is found (1)
- prevention: limit login attempts / lock account / long complex passwords / 2FA / CAPTCHA (1)
scheme.model_answer: A program automatically tries every possible password until it finds the right one; locking the account after five wrong attempts prevents it.

parts.title: Ethical problem
parts.text: Analyse **one** ethical problem that arises if a pupil cracks the database and changes marks.

scheme.mark_scheme: Problem (1) + analysis (1), e.g. marks no longer reflect real work — unfair to other pupils / universities misled; other pupils' private data accessed — privacy violated; trust in the school system lost
scheme.model_answer: Changed marks would be unfair to pupils who earned their marks honestly, and universities would receive false information, so the whole assessment system could no longer be trusted.

parts.title: Ethical hacker
parts.text: The school hires a **white-hat** hacker. Explain how this differs from a black-hat hacker.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A white-hat hacker tests the system with the owner's permission to find and report weaknesses (1)
- a black-hat hacker breaks in illegally to steal or cause harm (1)
scheme.model_answer: The white-hat hacker has the school's permission and reports the weaknesses so they can be fixed, whereas a black-hat hacker breaks in illegally to steal data or cause damage.

questions.title: Confidential company data
questions.text: A company stores contracts and customers' personal data on its file server.

parts.title: Two measures
parts.text: Give **two** measures that the company can take to protect confidential data from being stolen.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two from: encrypting data (1); granting limited access rights (1); blocking access from certain locations (1); keeping logs of user entries to the system (1)
scheme.model_answer: 1 Encrypting the data. 2 Keeping logs of who opens which files.

parts.title: Authentication and authorisation
parts.text: Explain the difference between authentication and authorisation.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Authentication checks who the user is (password, biometrics) (1)
- Authorisation decides what the user is allowed to access / do (access rights) (1)
scheme.model_answer: Authentication checks the identity of the user, for example with a password; authorisation then decides which files that user may read or change.

parts.title: Least privilege
parts.text: Explain why each employee should be given access only to the data needed for their job.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Fewer people can see / change confidential data, so insider misuse or mistakes are less likely (1)
- if an account is cracked, the attacker can reach only a small part of the data (1)

points.criterion: Limits damage from a cracked account

scheme.model_answer: Fewer employees can see confidential data, so it is less likely to be leaked, and if one account is cracked the attacker can only reach the files that employee was allowed to use.

parts.title: Legal consequence
parts.text: State **one** legal consequence for the company if customers' personal data is stolen because it was not protected.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any one (1): fine under personal data protection law; legal action / compensation claims by customers; investigation by authorities
scheme.model_answer: It could be fined under the law on personal data protection.

questions.title: Malware
questions.text: Malware is a serious threat to organisations.

parts.title: Malware types
parts.text: Draw a line to link each type of malware to the problem it causes.

right.text: Files are encrypted until a payment is made
Passwords typed by the user are stolen
The network slows down as copies spread to every computer

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R1, L2–R2, L3–R3, L4–R4. One mark per correct line.

parts.title: Analyse ransomware
parts.text: An airline's booking system is infected with ransomware. Analyse the problems this causes for the airline and its passengers.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Any four developed points (1 each): bookings / check-in impossible — flights delayed or cancelled; passengers stranded / miss connections; airline loses income / pays compensation; cost of ransom or recovery, no guarantee of recovery; passengers' personal / payment data may be stolen — privacy, identity theft; reputation damage / loss of trust
[Max 4]
scheme.model_answer: Staff cannot check passengers in or sell tickets, so flights are delayed or cancelled and passengers are stranded. The airline loses income and must pay compensation, as well as the cost of restoring its systems or paying the ransom, which may not even return the data. Passengers' personal and card details may also have been stolen, putting them at risk of fraud, and the airline's reputation suffers.

questions.title: Privacy policies
questions.text:
An online learning platform publishes this extract from its privacy policy:

> *We collect your name, e-mail address and test results to personalise your lessons. We share your e-mail address with our partner who sends newsletters. Data is stored on servers in Kazakhstan for three years after your last login. You may ask us to correct or delete your data.*

parts.title: Purpose
parts.text: Explain the purpose of a privacy policy.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Informs users what personal data is collected and how it is used / stored / shared (1)
- so they can give informed consent / know their rights / required by law (1)
scheme.model_answer: It tells users which personal data is collected and how it is used and shared, so they can decide whether to agree and know their rights.

fields.label: The purpose of collecting the data
Which data is shared, and with whom
How long the data is kept

scheme.mark_scheme:
Purpose: to personalise lessons (1)
Shared: e-mail address with the newsletter partner (1)
Kept: three years after the last login (1)
scheme.model_answer: To personalise lessons; the e-mail address is shared with a newsletter partner; three years after the last login.

parts.title: Limitation
parts.text: Explain **one** reason why a privacy policy may not fully protect users.

scheme.mark_scheme: Reason (1) + explanation (1): users do not read long / legal policies so agree without understanding; must accept to use the service; company can change the policy; policy does not stop data being hacked / partner may misuse data
scheme.model_answer: Most users do not read long policies written in legal language, so they agree to their e-mail being shared without realising it.

summary: The ethical and legal problems caused by cracking (hacking) computer systems, how to protect data from unauthorised access, the problems caused by different types of malware, and what privacy policies are and what they contain.

blocks.content: **Gaining unauthorised access** to a computer system, network or data — by guessing or stealing passwords, exploiting software weaknesses or tricking people. **Cracking** usually means breaking into systems or breaking software protection **with malicious intent**.

items.title: Black-hat hackers (crackers)
items.content: Break into systems **illegally** for personal gain or to cause harm: stealing money or data, blackmail, sabotage.

items.title: White-hat (ethical) hackers
items.content: Security experts who test systems **with the owner's permission** (penetration testing) to find weaknesses and fix them before criminals exploit them.

items.title: Grey-hat hackers
items.content: Break in **without permission** but without criminal intent — e.g. to report a weakness. Still **illegal** and ethically questionable.

blocks.title: Common cracking methods
rows: A program tries **every possible password** until one works
Tries common words and leaked passwords
Tricks people into **revealing passwords** with fake e-mails, websites or phone calls
Uses **bugs in unpatched software** to get in
Types SQL code into a web form to read or change the database
Captures data sent over an **unencrypted** network, e.g. public Wi-Fi
Records the keys a user types, including passwords

theory.title: Ethical and legal problems of cracking

blocks.title: Problems caused by cracking
rows: **Identity theft** — criminals use stolen personal details
**Financial loss** — stolen money, fines, cost of recovery
Loss of **trust** in online banking, e-government, shopping
Theft of money from bank accounts
**Theft of confidential data** — customers' details, trade secrets
**Invasion of privacy** — private messages, photos published
Cost passed to everyone through higher prices and taxes

items.title: Why cracking is unethical
items.content:
- It **violates privacy** — people have a right to control their personal data.
- It is **theft** of property (data, money, intellectual property) even if nothing physical is taken.
- It **harms innocent people** — customers, patients, employees.
- It **breaks trust** between people and organisations.
- "I only looked, I did not change anything" is still **unauthorised access**.

items.title: Legal consequences
items.content:
- In Kazakhstan, unauthorised access to computer information is a crime under the **Criminal Code** (fines, correctional work, imprisonment).
- Organisations that fail to protect personal data can be fined under the **Law on Personal Data and its Protection**.
- Most countries have similar laws (e.g. the UK **Computer Misuse Act**, the EU **GDPR**).

blocks.title: Ethical dilemma — analyse it
blocks.content:
*A student discovers that the school's marking website lets anyone see every pupil's marks by changing a number in the address bar. She shows her friends.*

- **Ethical problem:** she accessed other pupils' **private data** without permission and shared it — a breach of their privacy.
- **Legal problem:** this is **unauthorised access**, even though the website was badly designed.
- **The right action:** report the weakness **privately** to the school's IT staff (responsible disclosure) without using or sharing the data.
- **The school's responsibility:** it failed to protect personal data and must fix the vulnerability.

blocks.title: Measures against unauthorised access
rows: Long passwords with upper and lower case, digits and symbols are much harder to guess or brute-force
A stolen password is not enough — a second factor (phone code, fingerprint) is needed
The account is locked after several wrong passwords → stops brute-force attacks
Each user can only read or change the data needed for their job (**principle of least privilege**)
Stolen or intercepted data cannot be read; **SSL/TLS (HTTPS)** protects data in transit
The database stores only a hash, so stolen password files do not reveal the passwords
Close the vulnerabilities that crackers exploit
Record who accessed what and when, so misuse is detected
**Blocking access from certain locations / IP addresses**
Only allows log-in from trusted networks or countries
Staff recognise phishing and do not share passwords
Locked server rooms, screen locks when staff leave their desks

blocks.title: Authentication vs authorisation
rows: Access rights: read, write, delete, execute
A teacher logs in with a password and code
The teacher can edit marks, a pupil can only view their own

blocks.title: Protecting a school database against cracking (exam style)
blocks.content:
- Enable **two-factor authentication** for staff.
- Increase **password complexity** and limit **login attempts**.
- Use the **SSL / TLS protocol** (HTTPS) so data is encrypted in transit.
- **Encrypt** stored data and **hash** passwords.
- Give pupils and teachers **different access rights**.
Software designed to **damage, disrupt or gain unauthorised access** to a computer system or data.

blocks.title: Types of malware and their effects
rows: Attaches to a program or file; spreads when the infected file is run or shared
Corrupts or deletes files, slows the computer
**Spreads by itself** across networks, without user action
Uses bandwidth, slows or crashes networks, carries other malware
Disguised as **useful software**; the user installs it
Opens a **back door** for crackers, steals data
Demands **payment** for the key; data loss, downtime
Annoying, slows the computer, may lead to dangerous sites
Lets a criminal control many infected computers
Hides other malware, gives full control to the attacker

items.title: Problems for individuals
items.content:
- **Loss of data** (photos, documents) and money (ransom, stolen bank details).
- **Identity theft** and invasion of privacy.
- Slow or unusable computer; cost of repair.

items.title: Problems for organisations and society
items.content:
- **Downtime** — hospitals, airlines or factories stop working (e.g. the WannaCry ransomware attack on hospitals in 2017).
- **Financial loss** — ransom, recovery, lost business, fines for leaked data.
- **Reputation damage** and loss of customer trust.
- Attacks on **critical infrastructure**; spread of spam and fake news through botnets.

blocks.title: Countermeasures
blocks.content: Anti-virus software with up-to-date signatures, firewalls, software updates, not opening unknown attachments or links, downloading only from trusted sources, limited user rights and **regular offline backups** (see **Data protection measures**).

A **legal document** published by an organisation (on its website or app) that **explains what personal data it collects, why it collects it, how it is used, stored and protected, who it is shared with, and what rights the user has**.

blocks.title: What a privacy policy contains
rows: Which personal data is collected: name, e-mail, phone, location, IP address, cookies, payment details
**Why** the data is collected: providing the service, processing orders, improving the website, advertising
Whether data is **shared with or sold to third parties** (advertisers, partners, government)
**How long** data is kept, **where** it is stored (country), how it is **protected** (encryption)
Which cookies are used and how to switch them off
The right to **access, correct, delete** the data, to withdraw **consent**, to complain
Special rules for users under a certain age
Who to contact about data, and how users are told about changes to the policy

items.title: Why privacy policies are needed
items.content:
- **Laws require them** — e.g. the Kazakhstan Law on Personal Data and its Protection, the EU GDPR.
- Users can make an **informed decision** before giving their data (**consent**).
- They make organisations **accountable** for how they use data.
- They build **trust** between users and the organisation.

items.title: Problems with privacy policies
items.content:
- Often **very long and written in legal language**, so most people do not read them.
- Users must often accept them to use the service ("take it or leave it").
- Policies can **change**, and data already given may be used in new ways.
- A policy does not guarantee the data is actually secure.

blocks.title: Reading a privacy policy (exam style)
blocks.content:
An app's policy says: *"We collect your location to show nearby shops. We share anonymised location data with advertising partners. Data is kept for 12 months. You can delete your account at any time."*
- **Data collected:** location.
- **Purpose:** to show nearby shops.
- **Sharing:** anonymised data given to advertisers.
- **Storage period:** 12 months.
- **User right:** to delete the account.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: The school database is always at risk of system cracking. Write ways to protect against cracking. [2]**
Enable **two-factor authentication** (1); increase **password complexity** / limit login **attempts** / use the **SSL protocol** / **encrypt** the data / **hash** passwords (1).

**Q: Give two measures that the company can take to protect confidential data from being stolen. [2]**
**Encrypting** data (1); granting **limited access rights** (1). *(Also: blocking access from certain locations, keeping logs of user entries.)*

**Q: Analyse one ethical problem that arises when a hacker cracks a hospital system. [2]**
Patients' **confidential medical records** may be exposed or sold (1), violating their **privacy** and possibly causing discrimination or blackmail; treatment may also be **delayed** if systems stop working, putting lives at risk (1).

**Q: Explain the purpose of a privacy policy. [2]**
It **tells users what personal data is collected and how it is used, stored and shared** (1), so that they can give **informed consent** and know their **rights** (1).

- Saying a **firewall** removes viruses, or that **anti-virus** blocks hackers — say what each one actually does.
- Confusing a **virus** (needs a host file and user action) with a **worm** (spreads on its own).
- Describing a privacy policy as "a policy about privacy" — say **what it contains**.
- Giving consequences without **analysing** them: *who* is harmed and *how*.

blocks.title: Check yourself
items: What is the difference between black-hat, white-hat and grey-hat hackers?
Name four cracking methods and a countermeasure for each.
Give two ethical and two legal problems caused by cracking.
Explain the difference between authentication and authorisation.
Describe five types of malware and the problems each causes.
List six things a privacy policy should explain.

topic_exam.instructions: Answer **all** questions. The number of marks is given in brackets [ ] at the end of each part. Total: 30 marks. Time: 40 minutes.
